newsitem.title: USA: Westinghouse announces plan to split in two.
newsitem.headline: Westinghouse announces plan to split in two.

text.p: Westinghouse Electric Corp. made the long-awaited announcement Wednesday that it was splitting itself into a broadcast company and a traditional industrial business that would be distributed to shareholders.

The company, which will concentrate on its rapidly growing television and radio businesses, said the $4.6 billion spinoff will create a new Pittsburgh-based company that will be called Westinghouse Electric Co., or Welco.

Westinghouse, a century-old conglomerate, said it would eliminate 1,100 jobs as part of the restructuring, for which it was taking a one-time charge of $125 million to cover severance and related costs.

After the spinoff, the current parent company will include the CBS Inc. television network, Group W Satellite Communications Co., a cable television marketing and distribution company, and Infinity Broadcasting, a radio broadcaster that Westinghouse is acquiring.
The broadcast company, to be headquartered in New York, will have its own board of directors and be headed by current Westinghouse Chairman Michael Jordan.
A new chief executive will be named for Welco, which will be based in Pittsburgh and have its own board, management and stock.
The breakup of Westinghouse offers investors the "pure media play" they have craved ever since the company acquired CBS for $5.4 billion nearly a year ago.
While Westinghouse's broadcast business will still be shackled to roughly $6 billion in debt, the escape from its slow growing industrial sibling won praise from analysts, if not investors.

"You're going to end up with an unencumbered opportunity for a direct play at the media company," said analyst Nicholas Heymann. "The company has a tremendous amount of potential and it's just a question of executing it."
"This is now a more focused company and you're better off owning a focused company," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker.
The company's stock fell $1.25 to $19.375 in heavy trading on the New York Stock Exchange after it had run up ahead of the widely expected announcement.
Analysts also said the new industrial company had to revamp lackluster operations to make itself attractive to investors.
But they also said the company could be investment-worthy if it pursued lucrative overseas contracts for its power business and used its one money-making unit, Thermo King, to bolster results.
"There's nothing there to draw investors, except the potential that (the new company) can turn around," said Greg Drahuschak at Janney Montgomery Scott.
The new company will consist of four units -- power generation, energy systems, government operations and Thermo King.
"The biggest earnings potential (for Welco) is in overseas projects for the power business," said Greg Drahuschak at Janney Montgomery Scott.
"Westinghouse has been pursuing those projects and will continue to do so, I'm sure. The company has to have patience and hopefully enough cash flow until it turns around."
Westinghouse plans to offer up to 20 percent of its Thermo King refrigeration unit in a public stock offering to help finance the new industrial company.

The company also said it was divesting its Security Systems businesses and restructuring its Pittsburgh corporate headquarters and other industrial businesses to cut Welco's overhead and operating costs significantly.

Westinghouse said its breakup, which is expected to take nine months, is subject to a ruling from the Internal Revenue Service that the transaction will not be taxable to Westinghouse's shareholders or to Westinghouse.
The broadcast company will retain all debt obligations of the current Westinghouse Electric Corp., as well as the company's $1.8 billion operating losses that can be used as tax deductions.
